A guest lecture by **Ulf Strömberg** (University of Gothenburg; Professor of Epidemiologic Methods for over 20 years; leader of the Forte-funded **GeoTIME** programme, *Geomapping for Targeted Interventions and Methods for Evaluation*). It shows the methods of the course **applied to a real public health question**: geographic and socioeconomic inequalities in how and when cancer is detected in Sweden.

## Before you start
Bayesian disease mapping and exceedance probabilities ([4.16](session4.qmd#t4-16)), and the step from association to intervention ([6.21](session6.qmd#t6-21)–[6.29](session6.qmd#t6-29)).
:::

## 7.1 Identify: which outcomes show inequality in cancer detection? {#t7-1 .topic flag="inferred"}

::: {.core}
**In short.** The Canvas post names three outcomes whose geography can reveal inequity: **cancer incidence**, **stage at diagnosis** and **screening participation**. Each needs its own likelihood and denominator.
:::

| Outcome | What a geographic pattern can mean | Data structure → likelihood ([4.2](session4.qmd#t4-2)) |
|---|---|---|
| **Incidence** | Differences in risk factors, or in how much is detected | New cases over person-time or vs expected (age-standardized) → Poisson |
| **Stage at diagnosis** | Late detection: barriers to care, low awareness, low screening uptake | Advanced-stage cases among all diagnosed cases → Binomial |
| **Screening participation** | Unequal use of a free, organised programme | Participants among those invited → Binomial |

A key point for interpretation: **higher incidence is not always worse.** Where more people are screened, more early cancers are found, so incidence can be *higher* in areas with *better* detection. Stage at diagnosis and participation are closer measures of equity in **detection**.

::: {.exam-say}
**On the exam, be able to say:** Inequity in cancer detection can be studied through incidence, stage at diagnosis and screening participation. Stage and participation are proportions (Binomial); incidence is a rate or an observed-vs-expected count (Poisson). Higher incidence can reflect better detection.
:::

## 7.2 Small-area data: geographic and socioeconomic inequalities together {#t7-2 .topic flag="inferred"}

::: {.core}
**In short.** Small-area data (for example DeSO, [1.4](session1.qmd#t1-4)) can show **where** detection is worse and whether that follows **socioeconomic** gradients. The course's small-area issues all apply.
:::

- **Small numbers.** Late-stage cancers per small area are few, so crude proportions are unstable; smoothing ([2.6](session2.qmd#t2-6), [4.12](session4.qmd#t4-12)) and exceedance probabilities ([5.6](session5.qmd#t5-6)) separate signal from noise.
- **Area-level socioeconomic data** (income, education, country of birth) can be added as covariates or summarized with an index ([6.17](session6.qmd#t6-17)).
- **Ecological fallacy** ([1.11](session1.qmd#t1-11)): an area-level association between deprivation and low participation does not show that the deprived individuals are the ones not participating.
- **MAUP** ([1.10](session1.qmd#t1-10)): the inequality found can depend on the size and borders of the areas.

::: {.exam-say}
**On the exam, be able to say:** Small-area data can link geographic and socioeconomic inequalities in cancer detection, but bring the familiar problems: unstable small counts (use smoothing and exceedance probabilities), the ecological fallacy, and the MAUP.
:::

## 7.3 Inform and evaluate: geographically targeted interventions {#t7-3 .topic flag="inferred"}

::: {.core}
**In short.** Maps can **target** an intervention (for example extra screening invitations or outreach in areas with low participation). Whether it **worked** is a causal question: it needs the designs and cautions from [Session 6](session6.qmd#t6-21).
:::

The GeoTIME name says it: *geomapping for targeted interventions* **and** *methods for evaluation*.

| Step | Course tools | Caution |
|---|---|---|
| **Target**: choose areas | Disease mapping, exceedance probabilities, LISA hot spots | Use posterior probabilities, not crude extremes, so random noise does not decide where resources go |
| **Intervene** | | Targeted areas were chosen *because* they were worse: spatially structured confounding ([6.23](session6.qmd#t6-23)) and regression to the mean |
| **Evaluate** | Difference-in-differences, matching, comparison with untargeted areas ([6.25](session6.qmd#t6-25)) | Parallel trends; spillover to neighbouring areas ([6.27](session6.qmd#t6-27)) |

**Regression to the mean** (not on the slides): an area selected for an extreme value in one period tends to be less extreme in the next, even without intervention. A before–after comparison in the targeted areas alone would mistake this for an effect; a control group is needed.

::: {.exam-say}
**On the exam, be able to say:** Disease mapping can identify areas for targeted interventions (using posterior risks and exceedance probabilities), but evaluating the intervention is a causal question: the targeted areas were selected for being worse, so a design with comparable controls (for example DiD) is needed, with attention to spillovers and regression to the mean.
:::
